stimuli.title: Cooling the City, One Tree at a Time
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] On a July afternoon, the asphalt on a downtown parking lot can reach 150 degrees Fahrenheit, hot enough to burn bare skin in seconds. A few blocks away, the grass beneath a large oak may stay below 90 degrees. This difference helps explain a pattern that scientists call the urban heat island effect: cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, especially at night.

[2] The causes are built into the city itself. Dark roofs and roads absorb sunlight during the day and release that stored heat slowly after sunset. Buildings block breezes that would otherwise carry warm air away. Cars, air conditioners, and factories add heat of their own. In rural areas, by contrast, soil and plants hold moisture, and the evaporation of that moisture uses energy that would otherwise warm the air.

[3] Trees counter the heat island in two ways. First, their leaves shade the ground, keeping sunlight from reaching pavement and walls. Second, trees release water vapor through tiny pores in their leaves, a process called transpiration. Like sweat cooling a runner's skin, this evaporation draws heat from the surrounding air. A single mature tree can release more than 100 gallons of water on a hot day.

[4] In one recent study, researchers in a mid-sized city placed temperature sensors on lampposts in twelve neighborhoods. They found that blocks where trees covered at least 40 percent of the area were, on average, 5 degrees cooler on summer afternoons than blocks with less than 10 percent cover. The cooler blocks also used less electricity for air conditioning. The researchers cautioned, however, that the tree-lined blocks differed in other ways as well; many had newer homes with better insulation, which may account for part of the energy savings.

[5] Tree cover is rarely shared equally. In many cities, older neighborhoods with lower incomes have far fewer street trees than wealthier areas. Residents of these neighborhoods often have the least ability to pay for air conditioning, and they face the greatest risk of heat-related illness. For this reason, several cities now direct new plantings first to the blocks with the least shade.

[6] Planting a tree, though, is only the beginning. A young street tree needs regular watering for its first two to three years, and many newly planted trees die before they are established. A sapling also offers little shade; it may take fifteen years or more to grow a canopy wide enough to cool a block. Cities that plant thousands of trees without a plan to care for them may find that they have spent their budgets on trees that never reach maturity.

[7] None of this makes trees a quick fix. But for cities facing longer and hotter summers, few investments do as much for as long. A tree planted and cared for today will still be cooling the street for the children who grow up beneath it.

stimuli.title: The Last Night at the Blue Kettle
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] The bell above the door had rung for the last time at 9:40, when Mr. Abernathy came in for his pie. Now the diner was empty, and Marisol stood behind the counter with a rag in her hand, wiping a surface that was already clean.

[2] Her father sat in the corner booth, the one with the split seat he had patched three times with red tape. He was counting the register drawer, the way he had counted it every night for twenty-six years, though there was no reason to now. The bank already had the keys to the building. On Monday, men would come to haul away the grill.

[3] “You could leave that,” Marisol said.

[4] “I could.” He kept counting. His lips moved over the numbers, and when he finished, he wrote the total in the small green ledger and closed it with both hands, as if he were shutting a hymnal.

[5] She had spent most of her teenage years wanting to be anywhere else. The Blue Kettle had meant Saturday mornings refilling ketchup bottles while her friends slept, the smell of fryer oil caught in her hair at school, her father's voice calling “Order up!” over every conversation she tried to have. When she left for college, she had not looked back at the sign from the bus window. She had been proud of that.

[6] Now she looked at everything. The coffee rings worn pale into the counter. The photographs over the register: a Little League team the diner had sponsored, a newspaper clipping about the blizzard when her father had kept the grill going for stranded truckers, a picture of her own small face, frosting on her chin, at her sixth birthday in booth four.

[7] “Mr. Abernathy left a tip,” her father said. “Twenty dollars on a pie.”

[8] “That's generous.”

[9] “That's goodbye.” He slid the bill across the table toward her. “Put it in the jar.”

[10] The tip jar sat beside the register, a pickle jar with a hand-lettered label: FOR MARISOL'S COLLEGE. The label had yellowed and curled at one corner. She had been embarrassed by it once, too. She had graduated four years ago.

[11] “Papa, I finished college.”

[12] “I know.” He smiled for the first time all evening. “Some habits a man keeps because he needs them, not because they make sense.”

[13] She folded the bill and pushed it into the jar. Then she picked up the rag again and began wiping the counter, slowly, from one end to the other, the way he had taught her when she was twelve.

The new course is divided into four modules. Each of the modules (2) about ninety minutes to complete. During the course, you will learn to inspect a forklift before each shift, (3), and to report hazards immediately.

Classes will be held in the break room on Tuesday and Thursday (4) from our insurance provider will lead each one. Because so many employees will be in training at once, the class schedule will (5) how we assign shifts during April.

stimuli.title: Bringing the Mail to the Farm
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] At the end of the 1800s, most Americans still lived in rural areas, yet the nation's mail system largely ignored them. City residents had enjoyed free home delivery since 1863. Farm families, by contrast, had to travel to the nearest post office to collect their letters and newspapers, sometimes a round trip of several hours by wagon over dirt roads. During planting and harvest seasons, many farmers simply let their mail pile up for weeks.

[2] Farm organizations such as the National Grange argued that this arrangement was unfair. Rural Americans paid the same postage as city dwellers, they pointed out, but received far less service. In 1896, after years of pressure, the Post Office Department began an experiment: carriers would deliver mail along a handful of rural routes in West Virginia. The test proved popular, and new routes spread quickly. In 1902, Rural Free Delivery became a permanent service.

[3] The effects reached far beyond the mailbox. Because carriers could not travel on roads that were impassable in wet weather, the Post Office often refused to establish a route until local roads were improved. Communities that wanted delivery began grading and graveling their roads, and many counties raised taxes to pay for the work. In this way, the mail helped drive the “good roads” movement that later served automobiles.

[4] Delivery also changed what rural families read and bought. With a daily newspaper arriving at the farm gate, farmers could follow crop prices and national news as closely as city residents did. Mail-order catalogs from companies such as Sears, Roebuck and Montgomery Ward offered clothing, tools, and household goods at prices that small-town stores often could not match. When the Post Office began carrying packages through its parcel post service in 1913, those catalogs became even more important to rural households.

[5] Not everyone welcomed these changes. Many small-town merchants opposed rural delivery and, later, parcel post. They worried that customers who no longer needed to come to town for their mail would also stop coming to shop. Some warned that the government was helping large city companies at the expense of local businesses. Their fears were not entirely wrong: over the following decades, many rural general stores struggled to compete.

[6] Today, rural delivery is so ordinary that it is easy to overlook. Yet for millions of Americans at the turn of the twentieth century, a mailbox at the end of the lane meant something new: a daily connection to the rest of the country.

stimuli.title: Speed Cameras Save Young Lives
stimuli.source: By Dr. Lena Marsh, transportation safety researcher. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Every school day, thousands of children cross busy streets on their way to class. Most drivers slow down when they see a school-zone sign. Too many do not. Automated speed cameras, which photograph the license plates of vehicles exceeding the posted limit, are one of the most effective tools we have to protect those children, and every community with dangerous school zones should consider them.

The evidence from cities that use them is strong. When the city of Brenton installed cameras in twenty school zones in 2021, its transportation department measured traffic before and after. Average speeds during school hours fell from 31 miles per hour to 23 miles per hour in zones posted at 20. Over the next two years, crashes involving pedestrians in those zones dropped from 14 to 6. During the same period, school zones without cameras saw almost no change, which suggests that the cameras, and not some other factor, made the difference.

Speed matters because physics is unforgiving. A car traveling at 30 miles per hour carries more than twice the energy of one traveling at 20. Traffic safety research has consistently found that a pedestrian struck at a lower speed is far more likely to survive. A few miles per hour can be the difference between a broken arm and a funeral.

Critics claim that cameras are simply a way for cities to raise money. The record in Brenton says otherwise. Ticket revenue fell by more than half after the first year, because drivers learned to slow down. State law there also requires that camera revenue be spent only on traffic safety projects, such as crosswalks and sidewalk repairs. A program designed to make money would not be built to shrink.

Others raise concerns about privacy. These concerns deserve answers, and well-designed programs provide them. Brenton's cameras operate only during school hours, photograph only vehicles that exceed the limit by at least 6 miles per hour, and delete images after 90 days unless a ticket is contested. Drivers also received warnings, not fines, during the program's first month.

No single tool will make every street safe. Crossing guards, better signs, and redesigned roads all have a role. But cameras never get tired, never look away, and treat every driver the same. When the safety of children is at stake, we should use the tools that the evidence shows are working.

stimuli.title: School Zone Cameras Are the Wrong Answer
stimuli.source: By Ray Dutton, small-business owner and parent. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
No one is against safe school zones. I am a father of three, and I want every child to get to school safely. But automated speed cameras are not about safety. They are about money, and they treat ordinary, careful drivers like criminals.

Look at what happened in the town of Millbrook, just down the highway. In its first year, Millbrook's camera program collected over $1.2 million in fines. That is not a safety program. That is a tax disguised as a ticket. Once a city gets used to that kind of money, it will never give it up.

I know how these cameras work because one of them caught me. Last fall I received a $75 ticket in the mail for driving 31 in a 25 zone at 7:50 in the morning. There was not a single child on the sidewalk. I am a careful driver who has never been in an accident, and a police officer would have used common sense. A camera cannot.

Cameras also punish the wrong people. The ticket goes to whoever owns the car, not to whoever was driving it. If your teenager borrows your car and speeds, you pay. That is not how justice is supposed to work in this country.

People in our community do not want these cameras. When a neighborhood group posted a poll on its social media page last month, 78 percent of the people who responded said they were against the plan.

And where does it end? Today it is cameras in school zones. Tomorrow it will be cameras on every corner, tracking where we go and when. Once we accept being watched, we will never get our privacy back.

If we really want to protect children, we should hire more crossing guards and put more police officers near schools. An officer can stop a drunk driver or a reckless one. An officer can tell the difference between a dangerous driver and a parent going a few miles over the limit on an empty street. A camera only sees a number.

stimuli.title: It's Time to Bring Back Shop Class
stimuli.source: An opinion essay. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Walk through many American high schools today and you will find computer labs, college-counseling offices, and test-prep classrooms. What you are less likely to find is a room full of table saws, welding torches, or engine blocks. Over the past three decades, many districts have quietly closed their shop programs. That was a mistake, and it is one we can still correct.

[2] The first reason to restore these classes is practical: employers need the skills they teach. In a survey of 300 manufacturers in our region last year, nearly two-thirds reported that they had turned down new orders because they could not hire enough skilled workers. Electricians, plumbers, and machinists are retiring faster than young people are replacing them. These are not low-wage jobs; many pay more than positions that require a four-year degree, and they come without years of student debt.

[3] Second, hands-on classes reach students whom traditional classrooms often lose. My nephew struggled through ninth grade, convinced he was “bad at math.” Then he took an introductory construction class. Suddenly fractions mattered: an eighth of an inch was the difference between a cabinet door that closed and one that didn't. By his senior year, he was earning B's in geometry. Teachers in programs like his tell similar stories. A study of one state's career and technical programs found that students who took several such courses were more likely to graduate from high school than similar students who took none.

[4] Critics argue that shop classes are expensive. Equipment costs money, and so do the safety training and insurance that come with it. These concerns are real, but they are not insurmountable. Local businesses and trade unions are often eager to donate equipment and send volunteer instructors, because they benefit directly from a pipeline of trained graduates. Some districts share a single, well-equipped career center among several high schools, which spreads the cost.

[5] Others worry that shop classes will steer some students, especially students from low-income families, away from college. That danger is worth taking seriously. The answer, however, is not to eliminate the classes but to make them open to everyone and to make sure that no student is forced into them. A future engineer benefits from learning to weld just as much as a future welder benefits from learning algebra.

[6] We ask students to imagine their futures, and then we offer most of them only one road. Bringing back shop class would give them another, one that is just as respectable and, for many, just as rewarding.

stimuli.title: After the Storm
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] The storm had come through in the night, and by morning the Hendersons' fence lay flat across the yard like a row of dominoes. Eli saw it from the kitchen window while he was eating cereal, and he saw old Mr. Pruitt from next door already out there in his rubber boots, lifting a section of pickets and frowning at it.

[2] Eli did not like Mr. Pruitt. Nobody on Carver Street did, exactly. He complained when kids cut across his lawn, and he had once called the city about the Hendersons' music. When Eli's basketball rolled into his yard last summer, Mr. Pruitt had kept it for three days before leaving it on Eli's porch with a note: PLEASE BE MORE CAREFUL. The word PLEASE had been underlined twice, which somehow made it worse.

[3] “Go help him,” Eli's mother said, without looking up from her coffee.

[4] “It's not even his fence.”

[5] “The Hendersons are at their daughter's until Sunday. Go.”

[6] Outside, the air smelled like wet leaves and cut wood. Mr. Pruitt glanced up as Eli crossed the grass. He did not say hello. He handed Eli one end of a fence section and said, “Hold it straight. Straight. There.”

[7] They worked for most of the morning. Mr. Pruitt had a coffee can full of nails and a hammer with a handle worn smooth and dark where his hand went. He drove each nail in three strokes, tap, tap, bang, and never bent one. Eli bent four. After the fourth, Mr. Pruitt took the hammer, showed him how to hold it lower on the handle, and gave it back without a word.

[8] Near noon they stood back to look. The fence was not perfect. One post leaned a little, and a few pickets were shorter than the rest. But it stood.

[9] “Henderson's going to think the wind blew it back up,” Mr. Pruitt said. It took Eli a moment to understand that this was a joke. Then Mr. Pruitt did something Eli had never seen him do. He laughed, a short, rusty sound, like a gate that had not been opened in a long time.

[10] That evening, Eli found a hammer on his porch, its handle worn smooth and dark. A note was tucked beneath it. It said only: THANKS. Nothing was underlined.

stimuli.title: Harbor Point Grocery Employee Handbook, Section 6: Requesting Time Off
stimuli.source: Original workplace document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
6.1 Purpose. This section explains how employees request paid time off (PTO) and how requests are approved. Following these steps helps us keep every department staffed while giving employees the time they have earned.

6.2 Earning PTO. Full-time employees earn 4 hours of PTO for every two-week pay period worked. Part-time employees who work at least 20 hours per week earn 2 hours per pay period. New employees begin earning PTO on their first day but may not use it until they have completed 90 days of employment.

6.3 How to Request PTO.

  1. Check your current PTO balance on the employee portal or on your most recent pay stub.
  2. Submit a request through the employee portal at least 14 days before the first day you plan to take off. Requests for three or more consecutive days must be submitted at least 30 days before the first day off.
  3. Your department manager will approve or deny the request within 5 business days. You will receive the decision by email.
  4. Once approved, the time off will appear on the posted schedule. If you need to cancel approved time off, notify your department manager as soon as possible.

6.4 Busy Periods. Because of high customer demand, PTO requests for the week of Thanksgiving and for the two weeks before December 25 are approved only in special circumstances. Employees who wish to take time off during these periods should speak with the store manager before submitting a request.

6.5 Unplanned Absences. If you are sick or have an emergency, call your department manager at least 2 hours before your shift begins. You may use available PTO for an unplanned absence. An absence without a call is treated as a no-show, and two no-shows within 12 months may result in disciplinary action.

6.6 Unused PTO. Up to 40 hours of unused PTO may be carried over into the next calendar year. Any balance above 40 hours on December 31 is forfeited and will not be paid out.

6.7 Questions. Questions about PTO balances should be directed to the payroll office. Questions about scheduling should be directed to your department manager.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Urban heat islands are caused mainly by heat from cars, air conditioners, and factories.
Cities should replace paved surfaces with grass and soil to bring summer temperatures down.
Trees can cool cities and protect vulnerable residents, but only when they are placed fairly and cared for over many years.
Neighborhoods with more trees use less electricity because their homes tend to be newer and better insulated.
items.explain:
The passage explains how trees cool cities (paragraphs 3–4), argues that new trees should go first to the least-shaded, most at-risk blocks (paragraph 5), and warns that young trees need years of care (paragraph 6). The conclusion sums this up: trees are not “a quick fix,” but a tree “planted and cared for” pays off for decades.

Cars and air conditioners are only one of several causes listed in paragraph 2. The passage never recommends replacing pavement with grass. The point about newer homes is a single caution in paragraph 4, not the main idea.

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, why does the author compare transpiration to “sweat cooling a runner's skin”?
options: to explain an unfamiliar process by connecting it to a familiar experience
to argue that trees, like athletes, need extra water in hot weather
to show that transpiration cools the air faster than shade does
to suggest that people should exercise under trees during the summer
items.explain:
Transpiration is a scientific term most readers do not know. Almost everyone knows that sweating cools the body as the sweat evaporates, so the comparison helps the reader understand that evaporation from leaves “draws heat from the surrounding air” in the same way.

The comparison is not about trees needing water (that idea appears in paragraph 6, for a different reason), and the passage never compares the speed of transpiration and shade or gives advice about exercise.

items.prompt: Paragraph 4 is shown below. Click the sentence that suggests the energy savings on tree-lined blocks may not be caused by the trees alone.
spans: In one recent study, researchers in a mid-sized city placed temperature sensors on lampposts in twelve neighborhoods.
They found that blocks where trees covered at least 40 percent of the area were, on average, 5 degrees cooler on summer afternoons than blocks with less than 10 percent cover.
The cooler blocks also used less electricity for air conditioning.
The researchers cautioned, however, that the tree-lined blocks differed in other ways as well; many had newer homes with better insulation, which may account for part of the energy savings.
items.explain:
The last sentence warns that the tree-lined blocks “differed in other ways as well,” and that newer homes with better insulation “may account for part of the energy savings.” That is another possible cause, so the trees may not be the only reason electricity use was lower.

The third sentence reports the lower electricity use but does not question its cause.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 5, why do several cities now plant trees first on the blocks with the least shade?
options: Land on those blocks is less expensive for cities to buy.
Residents there face the greatest heat risk and are often least able to pay for air conditioning.
Young trees grow more quickly in older neighborhoods.
Residents of wealthier areas have asked cities to stop planting trees.
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 says that residents of low-shade neighborhoods “often have the least ability to pay for air conditioning, and they face the greatest risk of heat-related illness,” and then says “For this reason” cities plant there first.

The passage says nothing about land prices, growth rates in different neighborhoods, or complaints from wealthier areas.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by paragraph 6?
options: Young trees provide most of their cooling during their first three years.
Cities should stop planting trees until their budgets increase.
Most newly planted street trees die within fifteen years.
The success of a tree-planting program depends on caring for young trees after they are planted.
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 says planting “is only the beginning,” that young trees need watering for two to three years, and that cities without “a plan to care for them” may waste their budgets on trees “that never reach maturity.” Care after planting is what makes the program succeed.

The paragraph says the opposite of the first choice (a sapling “offers little shade”). It never tells cities to stop planting. It says “many” new trees die before they are established, not “most,” and the fifteen-year figure is about how long a canopy takes to grow, not about trees dying.

items.prompt: How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?
options: Paragraph 2 explains what makes cities hot, and paragraph 3 explains how trees work against those causes.
Paragraph 3 presents evidence that contradicts the causes listed in paragraph 2.
Paragraph 3 describes a study whose results are summarized in paragraph 2.
Paragraph 2 makes a claim about trees that paragraph 3 proves with statistics.
items.explain:
Paragraph 2 opens, “The causes are built into the city itself,” and lists them: dark surfaces absorbing sunlight, blocked breezes, added heat, and a lack of moisture to evaporate. Paragraph 3 opens, “Trees counter the heat island in two ways”: shade keeps sunlight off pavement, and transpiration adds the cooling evaporation that cities lack. This is a problem-and-response structure.

Paragraph 3 does not contradict paragraph 2, and the study appears in paragraph 4, not paragraph 3.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the father counts the register drawer “though there was no reason to now.” What does this detail suggest about him?
options: He suspects that money is missing from the register.
He must give the bank a final record of the diner's earnings.
He is holding on to a familiar routine as the diner closes.
He wants to teach Marisol how to manage the diner.
items.explain:
He counts the drawer “the way he had counted it every night for twenty-six years,” even though the diner is closing for good. Later he explains himself: “Some habits a man keeps because he needs them, not because they make sense” (paragraph 12). The routine comforts him.

Nothing in the story suggests missing money or a report owed to the bank, and the narrator says there was “no reason” to count, which rules out a required task.

items.prompt: In paragraph 4, the father closes the ledger “with both hands, as if he were shutting a hymnal.” This comparison suggests that he—
options: is too tired to handle the ledger with one hand
treats the end of his work at the diner with seriousness and respect
plans to attend a church service after the diner closes
worries that the old ledger will fall apart
items.explain:
A hymnal is a book of songs used in worship, and people close it with care. Comparing the ledger to a hymnal shows that the father treats this final count almost as a ceremony, with reverence for twenty-six years of work.

The comparison describes his manner, not literal plans to go to church, and nothing in the story says he is exhausted or that the ledger is falling apart.

items.prompt: How does Marisol's attitude toward the diner change over the course of the story?
options: She once loved working there but now resents the time it took from her.
She once felt proud of the diner but now feels embarrassed by its worn condition.
She once ignored the diner but now wants to find a way to keep it open.
She once wanted to get away from it but now pays close attention to its details and memories.
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 says she “spent most of her teenage years wanting to be anywhere else” and was proud she “had not looked back” when she left. Paragraph 6 begins, “Now she looked at everything,” and lists the coffee rings, photographs, and her birthday picture.

The first two choices reverse the change. Nothing suggests she wants to keep the diner open; the bank already has the keys.

items.prompt: Which details from the story best support the idea that the Blue Kettle was important to its community? Select two answers.
options: a photograph of a Little League team the diner had sponsored
the corner booth's split seat, patched three times with red tape
a newspaper clipping about the father keeping the grill going for stranded truckers during a blizzard
the bank already having the keys to the building
the smell of fryer oil caught in Marisol's hair at school
the yellowed label on the tip jar
items.explain:
Sponsoring a Little League team and feeding stranded truckers during a blizzard (paragraph 6) both show the diner serving people beyond the family. The newspaper clipping also shows the town took notice.

The patched seat, the bank's keys, the fryer-oil smell, and the tip-jar label tell us about the diner's age, its closing, and the family's life, not about its role in the community.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Since then, our team {{0}} two new dock levelers and a brighter lighting system, but equipment alone cannot prevent accidents.”

options: installs
will install
has installed
installing

items.explain:
“Since then” describes an action that began in the past (last spring) and connects to the present, which calls for the present perfect tense: has installed.

“Installs” (present) and “will install” (future) do not fit a time period that started in the past, and “installing” cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence by itself.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Each of the modules {{0}} about ninety minutes to complete.”

options: take
takes
are taking
have taken

items.explain:
The subject is Each, which is singular. “Of the modules” is a prepositional phrase and does not change the subject. A singular subject needs a singular verb: Each … takes.

“Take,” “are taking,” and “have taken” are plural forms that wrongly agree with “modules.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“During the course, you will learn to inspect a forklift before each shift, {{0}}, and to report hazards immediately.”

options: balancing a load safely
a load should be balanced safely
to balance a load safely
you balance a load safely

items.explain:
Items in a series should have the same grammatical form. The other two items are infinitive phrases (“to inspect,” “to report”), so the middle item must be one too: to balance a load safely.

“Balancing” is an -ing form, and the other two choices are clauses, so they break the pattern.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Classes will be held in the break room on Tuesday and Thursday {{0}} from our insurance provider will lead each one.”

options: mornings, a trainer
mornings a trainer
mornings and, a trainer
mornings; a trainer

items.explain:
The sentence contains two independent clauses: “Classes will be held … on Tuesday and Thursday mornings” and “a trainer from our insurance provider will lead each one.” A semicolon correctly joins them: mornings; a trainer.

A comma alone creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and “and,” followed by a comma puts the comma in the wrong place.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Because so many employees will be in training at once, the class schedule will {{0}} how we assign shifts during April.”

options: affect
effect
affects
effecting

items.explain:
Affect is the verb meaning “to influence.” The schedule will influence how shifts are assigned. After the helping verb “will,” use the base form: “will affect.”

“Effect” is usually a noun meaning “a result.” “Affects” and “effecting” are the wrong forms to follow “will.”

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the memo. Choose the transition that best connects them.

“Most of you completed the old training within the past two years. {{0}}, the new course is required for everyone, regardless of when you last trained.”

options: Therefore
For example
However
Similarly

items.explain:
The first sentence might lead employees to think they can skip the course; the second says the course is required anyway. That is a contrast, so However is correct.

“Therefore” signals a result (recent training does not cause the requirement), “For example” introduces an example, and “Similarly” signals a likeness.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Team leads should remind {{0}} crews to sign up by March 20.”

options: there
their
they're
them

items.explain:
The crews belong to the team leads, so the possessive pronoun their is correct.

“There” refers to a place, “they're” means “they are,” and “them” is an object pronoun that cannot show ownership before a noun.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“{{0}} will answer any questions you have about the new course.”

options: Paul Reyes the assistant director of Human Resources
Paul Reyes, the assistant director of Human Resources
Paul Reyes, the assistant director of Human Resources,
Paul, Reyes the assistant director of Human Resources

items.explain:
“The assistant director of Human Resources” is an appositive: it renames Paul Reyes and adds extra information. Because the name already identifies the person, the appositive is set off with a comma on both sides, and the sentence continues with the verb: Paul Reyes, the assistant director of Human Resources, will answer.

With no commas, the appositive is not set off at all. With only the first comma, the appositive is never closed, so the sentence reads as if the subject runs straight into the verb without a break. A comma between a first and last name splits the name.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Rural Free Delivery connected farm families to the wider country and brought broad changes, though not everyone benefited.
Rural Free Delivery was created mainly to help companies such as Sears, Roebuck sell more goods.
Small-town merchants succeeded in slowing the spread of rural mail delivery.
The good roads movement began because automobiles needed better roads.
items.explain:
The passage describes the problem rural families faced (paragraph 1), the creation of Rural Free Delivery (paragraph 2), its effects on roads, reading, and shopping (paragraphs 3–4), the merchants who lost out (paragraph 5), and its meaning as “a daily connection to the rest of the country” (paragraph 6).

The service was created after pressure from farm groups, not to help catalog companies. The passage says new routes “spread quickly,” so merchants did not slow it. Paragraph 3 says the mail drove the good roads movement that “later served automobiles,” so automobiles did not start it.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 1?
options: to argue that rural residents should have paid lower postage rates
to describe the problem that Rural Free Delivery was created to solve
to explain why most Americans moved to cities by 1900
to show that farmers had little interest in reading the news
items.explain:
Paragraph 1 shows that city residents had home delivery while farm families had to travel hours to a post office and often let mail pile up. This sets up the problem that the rest of the passage shows Rural Free Delivery solving.

The postage complaint appears in paragraph 2 and was about equal service, not lower rates. Paragraph 1 says most Americans “still lived in rural areas.” Farmers let mail pile up because they were busy, not because they lacked interest; paragraph 4 shows they eagerly followed the news once it arrived.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, classify each statement as a cause that led to Rural Free Delivery or an effect that resulted from it. Drag each statement into the correct box.
choices: Farm families had to travel to a post office to collect their mail.
Farm groups argued that rural residents paid the same postage for less service.
Counties raised taxes to grade and gravel their roads.
Farmers could follow crop prices as closely as city residents did.
Many rural general stores struggled to compete.
items.explain:
Causes: The long trips to the post office (paragraph 1) and the Grange's argument that the arrangement was unfair (paragraph 2) came first and led to the 1896 experiment “after years of pressure.”

Effects: Road improvements paid for by new taxes (paragraph 3), daily newspapers that let farmers follow crop prices (paragraph 4), and the struggles of rural general stores “over the following decades” (paragraph 5) all came after delivery began.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 3, how did Rural Free Delivery contribute to the “good roads” movement?
options: Mail carriers were hired to build and repair rural roads.
The Post Office paid counties to pave roads used by automobiles.
Communities improved their roads because the Post Office often refused to start a route until the roads were improved.
Farmers demanded better roads so that they could drive to town to shop.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 states that the Post Office “often refused to establish a route until local roads were improved,” so communities that wanted delivery graded and graveled their roads and raised taxes to pay for it.

The passage says counties paid for the work themselves, not the Post Office, and carriers delivered mail rather than building roads. Shopping trips to town are the opposite of what delivery encouraged.

items.prompt: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word impassable most nearly means—
options: unpaved
expensive to repair
rarely used
impossible to travel over
items.explain:
The sentence says carriers “could not travel on roads that were impassable in wet weather.” The roads became impassable, impossible to get through, when they were wet. The word parts help too: im- (not) + pass + -able.

“Unpaved” is tempting because dirt roads are unpaved, but a dirt road is unpaved in dry weather too; the word describes what happens when the road becomes wet.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 5, why did many small-town merchants oppose rural delivery and parcel post? Select two answers.
options: They believed customers who no longer came to town for mail would also stop shopping there.
They thought mail carriers would damage local roads.
They believed the government was helping large city companies at the expense of local businesses.
They expected postage rates for their own businesses to rise.
They thought mail-order catalogs sold goods of lower quality.
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 gives two reasons: merchants “worried that customers who no longer needed to come to town for their mail would also stop coming to shop,” and some “warned that the government was helping large city companies at the expense of local businesses.”

The passage never mentions damage to roads, higher postage for merchants, or the quality of catalog goods.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author says that the merchants' fears “were not entirely wrong.” This statement shows that the author—
options: recognizes that rural delivery had real costs for some groups
agrees that rural delivery should have been stopped
believes the merchants exaggerated their fears to protect profits
thinks parcel post did more harm than good overall
items.explain:
The author follows the phrase with evidence: “over the following decades, many rural general stores struggled to compete.” The author admits the merchants were partly right about the costs while still presenting rural delivery positively overall, as “a daily connection to the rest of the country” (paragraph 6).

Nothing in the passage says delivery should have been stopped. “Not entirely wrong” means partly right, the opposite of saying the fears were exaggerated. The author never weighs parcel post's overall harm.

essay.prompt:
The articles present arguments from a supporter and a critic of automated speed cameras in school zones.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Type your response in the box. This task may require approximately 45 minutes to complete.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“I am writing to apply for the medical receptionist position advertised on your {{0}} website.”

options: clinics
clinic's
clinics'

items.explain:
The website belongs to one clinic (Harbor Family Clinic), so it needs the singular possessive: clinic's.

“Clinics” is a plural with no apostrophe, and “clinics'” is a plural possessive, which would mean several clinics share the website.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“For the past three years, I have worked as a front-desk assistant at Lakeside Dental Group{{0}} I check in patients, answer phones, and manage a calendar of more than sixty appointments a day.”

options: . Where
, where
; where
, where,

items.explain:
“Where I check in patients …” is a dependent clause that adds information about Lakeside Dental Group. Because it describes a specific, named place, it is set off with a comma: Group, where I check in patients.

A period turns the clause into a fragment. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and “where I check in …” cannot stand alone. A second comma after “where” wrongly separates the word from its own clause.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The skills I developed in that role {{0}} directly to the duties listed in your posting.”

options: relates
is relating
relate
has related

items.explain:
The subject is skills, which is plural. The words “I developed in that role” describe the skills but do not change the subject. A plural subject takes a plural verb: skills … relate.

“Relates,” “is relating,” and “has related” are singular forms that wrongly agree with “role.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“My supervisor and {{0}} redesigned the office's check-in process last year, which cut average wait times by ten minutes.”

options: me
myself
mine
I

items.explain:
The pronoun is part of the subject of the verb “redesigned,” so it must be a subject pronoun: I. Test it by removing “My supervisor and”: “I redesigned,” not “Me redesigned.”

“Myself” is used only when the subject has already been named (“I did it myself”), and “mine” is possessive.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“{{0}}, I learned to stay calm and courteous with every caller.”

options: Working with patients who were often anxious or in pain
Anxious or in pain, working with patients
Patients who were often anxious or in pain, working with them
Having worked with, patients often anxious or in pain

items.explain:
An introductory modifier describes the subject that comes right after the comma, which is I. “Working with patients who were often anxious or in pain, I learned …” correctly says that the writer worked with the patients.

“Anxious or in pain” would describe “I,” suggesting the writer was the one in pain. The other two choices are jumbled and do not form a clear modifier.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience could {{0}} your team.”

options: compliment
complementing
complement
compliments

items.explain:
Complement means “to complete or go well with.” The writer means that her experience would add to and fit well with the team. After the helping verb “could,” use the base form: “could complement.”

“Compliment” means “to praise,” which does not make sense here, and “complementing” and “compliments” are the wrong forms to follow “could.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“{{0}}, I have attached my résumé and two letters of reference.”

options: Nevertheless
In contrast
For example
As requested in your posting

items.explain:
The writer is explaining why she has attached documents: the job posting asked for them. As requested in your posting makes that connection clearly.

“Nevertheless” and “In contrast” signal a contrast with the previous sentence, but there is none. Attaching a résumé is not an example of the previous sentence, so “For example” does not fit.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the author's central claim?
options: Shop classes are more valuable than college-preparatory classes.
Students from low-income families should be encouraged to choose skilled trades.
High schools should restore shop classes because they meet workforce needs and help many students succeed.
Businesses, not schools, should be responsible for training skilled workers.
items.explain:
Paragraph 1 states that closing shop programs “was a mistake, and it is one we can still correct.” Paragraph 2 gives “the first reason” (employers need the skills) and paragraph 3 gives the second (hands-on classes reach students “whom traditional classrooms often lose”).

The author calls the trades “just as respectable,” not more valuable, than college. Paragraph 5 warns against steering low-income students away from college. Businesses are described as partners who donate equipment, not as replacements for schools.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the author notes that skilled trade jobs “come without years of student debt.” Why does the author include this detail?
options: to suggest that the trades can be a financially sound alternative to a four-year degree
to argue that college tuition should be free for all students
to show that employers pay for their workers' training
to criticize students who borrow money to attend college
items.explain:
The detail comes right after the claim that many trade jobs “pay more than positions that require a four-year degree.” Together, the two points argue that the trades make good financial sense: good pay without the cost of college loans.

The author never discusses free tuition, employer-paid training, or blaming students who borrow.

items.prompt: Why is the study described at the end of paragraph 3 stronger evidence than the story about the author's nephew?
options: The study was conducted by teachers who work in career programs.
The study compares many students with similar students, while the story describes the experience of one person.
The study shows that students in shop classes earn higher grades in geometry.
The study proves that shop classes are the only reason students graduate.
items.explain:
The study looked at students across “one state's career and technical programs” and compared them with “similar students who took none.” A comparison of many students is more reliable than one personal story, which could be unusual and comes from someone with a personal connection.

The passage does not say teachers ran the study. The geometry grades belong to the nephew's story, not the study. The study found students “were more likely to graduate,” which does not prove shop classes are the only reason.

items.prompt: Paragraph 4 is shown below. Click the sentence in which the author directly acknowledges that the critics' concerns are valid before responding to them.
spans: Critics argue that shop classes are expensive.
Equipment costs money, and so do the safety training and insurance that come with it.
These concerns are real, but they are not insurmountable.
Local businesses and trade unions are often eager to donate equipment and send volunteer instructors, because they benefit directly from a pipeline of trained graduates.
Some districts share a single, well-equipped career center among several high schools, which spreads the cost.
items.explain:
“These concerns are real” is the author's own admission that the critics have a point; the rest of that sentence (“but they are not insurmountable”) turns to the rebuttal.

The first two sentences present the critics' argument, and the last two sentences are the author's responses.

items.prompt: Which ways does the author suggest schools could reduce the cost of shop programs? Select two answers.
options: accepting donated equipment from local businesses and trade unions
charging students a fee for each class
sharing one well-equipped career center among several high schools
replacing hands-on equipment with computer simulations
reducing the number of college-counseling offices
items.explain:
Paragraph 4 names both solutions: businesses and unions “are often eager to donate equipment,” and some districts “share a single, well-equipped career center among several high schools, which spreads the cost.”

Student fees, simulations, and cutting counseling offices are never mentioned.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 5.

“A future engineer benefits from learning to weld just as much as a future welder benefits from learning algebra.”

What is the purpose of this sentence?
options: to argue that algebra should be removed as a graduation requirement
to show that welders earn as much as engineers
to admit that shop classes may steer students away from college
to support the idea that shop classes have value for all students, whatever their plans
items.explain:
The sentence comes right after the author proposes making shop classes “open to everyone.” It shows that hands-on skills help college-bound students too, just as academic skills help future tradespeople.

The sentence values algebra rather than removing it and says nothing about pay. The admission about steering students comes earlier in the paragraph (“That danger is worth taking seriously”); this sentence is part of the author's answer to that danger.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the word PLEASE in Mr. Pruitt's note “had been underlined twice, which somehow made it worse.” What does this detail suggest?
options: Eli did not understand why Mr. Pruitt had returned the basketball.
Mr. Pruitt had written the note in a hurry.
Eli read the note as a scolding rather than a polite request.
Eli's mother had asked Mr. Pruitt to write the note.
items.explain:
“Please” is normally polite, but underlining it twice adds stern emphasis. The phrase “made it worse” tells us Eli felt scolded. This fits the paragraph's list of reasons Eli “did not like Mr. Pruitt.”

The story does not say Eli was confused about the ball, that the note was rushed, or that Eli's mother was involved.

items.prompt: Paragraph 7 is shown below. Click the sentence that shows Mr. Pruitt helping Eli improve his work without speaking.
spans: They worked for most of the morning.
Mr. Pruitt had a coffee can full of nails and a hammer with a handle worn smooth and dark where his hand went.
He drove each nail in three strokes, tap, tap, bang, and never bent one.
After the fourth, Mr. Pruitt took the hammer, showed him how to hold it lower on the handle, and gave it back without a word.
items.explain:
In the last sentence, Mr. Pruitt “showed him how to hold it lower on the handle” and returned the hammer “without a word.” He teaches Eli silently.

The sentence about three strokes shows Mr. Pruitt's own skill, but he is not helping Eli in that sentence.

items.prompt: In paragraph 9, Mr. Pruitt's laugh is described as “a short, rusty sound, like a gate that had not been opened in a long time.” This comparison suggests that—
options: Mr. Pruitt is laughing at Eli's uneven work on the fence
Mr. Pruitt has not laughed often in a long time
Mr. Pruitt is sick from working in the wet weather
the Hendersons' gate was also damaged in the storm
items.explain:
A gate that has not been opened in a long time creaks and sticks. The simile suggests Mr. Pruitt's laugh is “rusty” from lack of use. This matches the previous sentence: laughing was “something Eli had never seen him do.”

He laughs at his own joke about the Hendersons, not at Eli. The comparison is figurative, so it says nothing about illness or a real gate.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Neighbors should avoid getting involved in one another's problems.
Storms and other disasters bring out the worst in people.
Young people should always obey their parents.
Working side by side can change how people see one another.
items.explain:
At the start, Eli “did not like Mr. Pruitt,” and his note felt like a scolding. After a morning of fixing the fence together, Eli sees Mr. Pruitt joke and laugh, and Mr. Pruitt gives Eli his own hammer with a note that says THANKS, with “Nothing … underlined” this time. The shared work changes how each sees the other.

The story shows the benefits of getting involved, not avoiding it, and the storm leads to kindness. Eli does obey his mother, but the story centers on what happens between Eli and Mr. Pruitt, not on obedience.

items.prompt: According to section 6.3, in what order do these steps happen when an employee requests PTO? Drag each step into the correct position.
choices: Receive an email with the manager's decision
See the approved time off on the posted schedule
Submit a request through the employee portal
items.explain: Section 6.3 lists the steps in order: (1) check your current PTO balance, (2) submit a request through the employee portal, (3) receive the manager's decision by email, and (4) once approved, see the time off on the posted schedule.

items.prompt: Lena, a full-time employee, wants to take off Monday, June 9, through Friday, June 13. According to the handbook, what is the latest date on which she can submit her request?
options: May 10
May 14
May 26
June 2
items.explain:
June 9 through June 13 is five consecutive days, so the 30-day rule in section 6.3 applies, counted from “the first day off,” June 9.

Count back: June 9 is 9 days after May 31, so 30 − 9 = 21 more days are needed in May. May 31 − 21 = May 10. Check: May 10 to May 31 is 21 days, plus 9 days to June 9, equals 30 days.

May 26 uses the 14-day rule, which is only for shorter requests. May 14 counts back from the last day off (June 13) instead of the first.

items.prompt: Kendra works 25 hours a week and was hired 60 days ago. Which statement about her PTO is accurate according to the handbook?
options: She does not earn PTO because she works part time.
She earns 4 hours of PTO for each pay period.
She is earning PTO but cannot use it for about 30 more days.
She may use her PTO now if her department manager approves.
items.explain:
Section 6.2 says part-time employees who work at least 20 hours a week earn PTO (2 hours per pay period), and Kendra works 25 hours. New employees earn PTO from their first day “but may not use it until they have completed 90 days.” 90 − 60 = 30 more days.

Part-time employees at 20 or more hours do earn PTO, but 2 hours per pay period, not 4. Manager approval does not override the 90-day rule.

items.prompt: According to section 6.4, which employee should speak with the store manager before submitting a PTO request?
options: an employee who wants to take off July 3
an employee who wants to take off December 20
an employee who needs to cancel approved time off
an employee who calls in sick two hours before a shift
items.explain:
Section 6.4 covers “the week of Thanksgiving and … the two weeks before December 25.” December 20 falls within the two weeks before December 25, so this employee should speak with the store manager first.

July 3 is not a busy period named in the handbook. Canceling approved time off goes to the department manager (section 6.3), and sick calls go to the department manager (section 6.5).
